question: Establishment Democrat?
headline: Mostly yes
summary: He entered the Senate by appointment from Gov. Gavin Newsom, launched his 2022 campaign with Chuck Schumer's and the DSCC's endorsement, won the California Democratic Party's endorsement, served as a DSCC vice chair for the 2024 cycle, and is the top Democrat on the Senate Rules Committee. He votes with Schumer {jeffAgree}% of the time. Of his {ndiff} splits with Schumer, {splitNoBills} are No votes on legislation Schumer backed, among them the March 2025 stopgap, the final FY2026 defense bill and the January 2026 funding packages; {splitYesBills} are Yes votes on legislation Schumer opposed, such as the GENIUS stablecoin bill; {splitYesNoms} are Yes votes on nominees Schumer opposed; and {splitNoNoms} are No votes on nominees Schumer backed.
why: "Mostly yes" because his path to the seat, his party roles and his voting record line up with Senate Democratic leadership and the state party. His independence shows in {ndiff} votes where he split from Schumer and in his Medicare for All cosponsorship.
tiles: Votes cast the same way as Chuck Schumer ({both} votes where both voted Yea or Nay)
Named to the Senate by Gov. Gavin Newsom in December 2020
One of two vice chairs of the Senate Democrats' campaign committee for the 2024 cycle
Top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, 119th Congress

e.text: Gov. Gavin Newsom selected him in December 2020 to fill the Senate seat Kamala Harris left to become Vice President.
Chuck Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee endorsed him when he launched his 2022 campaign in April 2021.
The California Democratic Party endorsed him in 2022 for both the special election and the regular election for a full term.
Served as one of two vice chairs of the DSCC for the 2024 cycle, named in January 2023 (news report).
Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration in the 119th Congress.
Votes the same way as Schumer on {jeffAgree}% of the {both} roll calls where both cast a Yea or Nay.
Money from Senate Democratic leaders' committees: {lead22} in 2021–22, {lead24} in 2023–24 and {lead26} in 2025–26, including {dscc} from the DSCC.

i.text: Broke with Schumer on {ndiff} votes, including voting against cloture on the March 2025 stopgap funding bill that Schumer voted to advance, against the final FY2026 defense authorization, and against the January 2026 appropriations packages.
Some breaks go the other way: he voted for the GENIUS stablecoin bill (S. 1582), which Schumer opposed.
Original cosponsor of Bernie Sanders' Medicare for All Act (S. 1506); Schumer is not a cosponsor.

timeline.text: Gov. Gavin Newsom selects him to fill Kamala Harris's Senate seat.
Sworn in as the first Latino to represent California in the U.S. Senate.
Launches his 2022 campaign with endorsements from Schumer and the DSCC.
The California Democratic Party endorses him for both 2022 Senate elections.
Named a DSCC vice chair for the 2024 cycle, with Sen. Tina Smith (news report).
Voted Nay on cloture on the March 2025 stopgap funding bill (H.R. 1968); Schumer voted Yea.
Voted Yea on passage of the GENIUS stablecoin bill (S. 1582); Schumer voted Nay.
Voted Nay on concurring in the House amendment to S. 1071, the final FY2026 defense authorization; Schumer voted Yea.
Voted Nay on the consolidated appropriations bill H.R. 6938; Schumer voted Yea.
Voted Nay on the further consolidated appropriations bill H.R. 7148; Schumer voted Yea.

left.text: He is an original cosponsor of the Medicare for All Act (S. 1506), and his 2022 campaign site listed Medicare for All among the issues he was fighting for.
